nodes.title: What neurodiversity means

nodes.scenario: A workplace is planning a 'neurodiversity awareness' event. Mira and Tavi are reviewing how the programme describes employees.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The draft says 'neurodiverse employees struggle with noisy offices'.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: That sounds too general. People have different sensory needs.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Should we say every neurodivergent person needs a quiet office?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No. Some people find a quiet room understimulating, and others benefit from it.

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Neurodivergence, a formal diagnosis and disability are related but distinct concepts. A population-level idea cannot be used to infer one person's traits.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Neurodiversity describes variation across a population. An individual's neurotype may inform support needs, but meaningful functioning emerges from the interaction between person and environment.

Another possibility: Some accommodations are widely useful across groups even when they are not universally needed; individualisation does not prohibit inclusive default design.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Ask which features of a task or environment create barriers, then evaluate whether the proposed adjustment removes them for the person concerned. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Neurodivergence, a formal diagnosis and disability are related but distinct concepts. A population-level idea cannot be used to infer one person's traits.
nodes.sources: Kapp et al. (2013), defining neurodiversity; WHO ICF (2001) disability and contextual functioning.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Ask which features of a task or environment create barriers, then evaluate whether the proposed adjustment removes them for the person concerned.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The findings strengthen a needs-led approach and weaken the assumption that diagnostic categories determine one uniform workplace preference.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

nodes.scenario: Tavi struggles to follow cross-talk in a busy meeting and asks for advance notes.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I contribute better when I can read the agenda beforehand.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Meetings are supposed to be about thinking on your feet.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The overlapping conversations make it hard to follow the current question.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Sometimes. Written notes and taking turns might be enough.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: So we could change the format without changing what the meeting is meant to achieve.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: The meeting format may create avoidable processing demands that limit Tavi's participation.
Tavi may not have enough background knowledge to contribute confidently.
The meaning of the event may differ between the speakers, even when they agree about the observable facts.
options.feedback: Different interpretations may contribute, but this is not yet specific enough to explain the response.

options.label: The immediate context may account for more of the reaction than a stable personal tendency would.
options.feedback: Situation-specific pressure is plausible, though the evidence may indicate an additional process.

options.label: A previous disagreement may have shaped the response, making the present conversation part of a longer pattern.
options.feedback: History could matter, but that earlier pattern has not yet been established.

nodes.body:
Neurodiversity describes variation across a population. An individual's neurotype may inform support needs, but meaningful functioning emerges from the interaction between person and environment.

Neurodivergence, a formal diagnosis and disability are related but distinct concepts. A population-level idea cannot be used to infer one person's traits.

glossary.definition: The fact that there is variation in how people's minds and nervous systems work across a population.
glossary.example: A university includes people with different attentional and sensory profiles.
glossary.limit: Neurodiversity refers to diversity across people; it is not a diagnosis assigned to one individual.

glossary.definition: A description of an individual's neurological functioning as differing from prevailing expectations.
glossary.example: A student identifies as autistic and describes a different sensory experience.
glossary.limit: The term does not establish the same abilities or support needs in every person.

glossary.definition: A clinical conclusion reached through a particular assessment process and criteria.
glossary.example: An adult undergoes an ADHD assessment exploring history and effects on daily life.
glossary.limit: Diagnosis and identity can overlap but are not interchangeable; support needs may exist without a diagnosis.

glossary.definition: How well the demands and features of a setting match what a person needs to function.
glossary.example: One worker concentrates better in a quiet room while another needs a little background sound.
glossary.limit: A useful adjustment is tested against actual barriers, rather than assigned only by diagnostic label.
